title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.

title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

title: Before you use it: Validating a tactical command vocabulary for multi-agent shooters
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning evaluates communication by its effect on task reward, which cannot separate messages that were understood and acted on from messages that were ignored while the policy improved for other reasons. Separating them needs a verdict on the individual message, and that needs a discrete command space—whose own validity is not usually examined. We freeze a tactical command vocabulary for Counter-Strike (28 verbs, 7,936 legal messages, 6 compliance predicates) and, before using it, measure it against 270 professional matches: coverage, stated as the share of observed events the mechanics cannot produce; collapse, the structure surviving projection, swept over granularity rather than fixed; and predicate sharpness, evaluated counterfactually over each predicate's parameter space, needing no compliance labels. The action space expresses 87.7–89.2% of professional kills; symbolisation retains 1,305–1,533 effective utility usages and 31–32 reachable objectives, under saturation checks; the predicates accept 1.00–4.71 candidates over the map's real callout regions, giving chance floors of 3–25% that any reported compliance rate must be read against. Applied to the closest existing abstraction of this game, the same measurements corroborate two of its design claims and price a third. None of this requires an agent, and seven statements written into specifications and never checked were falsified along the way, three of them in the vocabulary file we release.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Machine Learning
authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Prerna Wayakole
Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine-learning approach for problems in which decisions are made repeatedly and their quality becomes clear through feedback. Instead of depending on a fixed collection of labelled answers, an RL agent interacts with an environment, observes its changing state, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its decision policy through experience. This review examines the basic RL framework and discusses deep reinforcement learning, offline learning, multi-agent systems, and human-guided learning. Applications in robotics, games, education, finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems are considered. The review also identifies sample inefficiency, computational cost, instability, delayed rewards, limited generalization, and safety as important challenges. The paper concludes by identifying research opportunities for efficient, reliable, explainable, and adaptable RL systems.

title: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.

title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.

title: Intelligent chess venue model design driven by technological revolution
abstract: Guided by the practical needs of refereeing, this paper constructs a framework for an intelligent arena system for board game competitions, with a core focus on officials’ work and deeply empowered by technology. The system integrates technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and edge computing to automate and intellectualize processes including arena setup, game recording, behavior monitoring, and result statistics. Key technological breakthroughs have been achieved in automatic piece setup before each round, real-time data synchronization, and AI-assisted adjudication. Practical deployment demonstrates that this system can reduce the overall competition workflow time by over 30%, decrease the referees' workload by 80%, and achieve an accuracy rate exceeding 95% in providing early warnings for complex situational judgments. This research not only provides a feasible path for the intellectualization of Xiangqi (Chinese chess) competitions, but its system architecture and technical solutions are also applicable to the development of intelligent arenas for other board sports.

title: Smart Education Platform: Based on Emotions Content Delivery Using ML
abstract: This project proposes a Smart Education Platform that dynamically adapts online learning content based on students’ real-time emotions to improve engagement and outcomes. Leveraging multimodal inputs—facial expressions detected via webcam using ResNet, speech sentiment analysis through Wav2Vec, and contextual surveys the system identifies states such as engagement, boredom, and annoyance. Integrated within a Flask based web application and Moodle, a reinforcement learning agent tailors interventions (quizzes, lessons, condensed material) by optimizing a reward function (+1 for engagement,-1 for negative emotions). Privacy is prioritized through webcam opt-out, on-device processing, and informed consent. The solution was validated on 20–50 learners using AffectNet and other datasets, achieving high accuracy with fivefold cross-validationThe system provide personal, scalable, and privacy-aware experiences in a variety of educational contexts, addressing the limitations for static learning platforms. A focus on emotional agility enhances efficiency and motivation, setting a standard for future massive deployment and human-centered digital learning.

title: From Trajectories to Experience: A Survey of Experience-Driven LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents record in their trajectories which strategies failed and how they recovered, yet an agent that resolves a problem in one episode may repeat the same diagnostic detour in the next. Work on reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition addresses this gap under different names, making methods and their gains hard to compare. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task-execution trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies; it may be a trajectory kept as a precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We review methods through four lifecycle functions: formation selects or derives candidate experience from trajectories, organization makes it accessible, utilization applies it to current decisions or internalizes it into model parameters, and maintenance admits, consolidates, revises, and retires it as evidence accumulates. A recurring source of failure is guidance that loses its link to its applicability conditions and supporting evidence: it is over-generalized during formation, misapplied during utilization, and left unrevised during maintenance. We organize evaluation around intrinsic experience quality, the experience utilization process, and downstream effects, and separate three improvement claims: fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism. The reviewed studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Across seven application settings, we derive recommendations on whether reuse justifies its cost, what to retain, how strongly experience should influence a task, and when to revise it. We close with eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to correcting propagated errors and testing whether gains accumulate.

A recurring source of failure is guidance that loses its link to its applicability conditions and supporting evidence: it is over-generalized during formation, misapplied during utilization, and left unrevised during maintenance. We organize evaluation around intrinsic experience quality, the experience utilization process, and downstream effects, and separate three improvement claims: fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism. The reviewed studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Across seven application settings, we derive recommendations on whether reuse justifies its cost, what to retain, how strongly experience should influence a task, and when to revise it. We close with eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to correcting propagated errors and testing whether gains accumulate.

title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, naïve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to naïve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.

title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
abstract: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

title: Formation of Individual Organization in an Artificial System with Associative Long-Term Memory and a Hierarchy of Significance
abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical functional model for the formation of individual organization in an artificial system, in which long-term memory is treated not as an external archive but as a historically changing structure that participates in the interpretation of new experience. The starting criterion is a working definition of personality as the internal organization of different properties of a system, structured according to a hierarchical principle of significance, anchored in memory, and manifested as a coherent whole under different circumstances. The model combines associative reconstruction from an incomplete cue, multilevel internal states, a mechanism by which stable attitudes and significance arise from the consequences of the system’s own experience, an explicit rule by which these attitudes influence the next choice, a model of the system’s own causal history as an additional hypothesis, and a separate consolidation mode. A longitudinal experiment is specified using initially identical systems, frozen-state measurements, a simple learning control, and separate causal interventions on memory content, links, and acquired attitudes. The architecture is a theoretical proposal; whether it is sufficient for the formation of functional personality remains to be tested experimentally. The model makes no claim about phenomenal consciousness or subjective experience.

title: From Detection to Investigation: A Survey of Foundation Models and Agents for Financial Fraud and Financial Crime
abstract: Foundation models are extending research on financial fraud and financial crime from isolated risk detection to document understanding, relational analysis, and investigative workflows. A gap nevertheless separates model outputs from candidate evidence and actionable conclusions. This survey examines advances in six families of foundation models: language, vision, speech, temporal, graph, and tabular models. It compares their roles and limitations along two dimensions: the risk-control lifecycle and the directness of the supporting evidence. Existing studies show that pretraining can support representation reuse and the processing of unstructured information, with direct validation in some financial tasks. Cross-modal identity binding, information availability over time, report faithfulness, and case-level benefits require separate evaluation. Evidence on investigative agents spans prototypes, controlled tasks, expert assessments, and industry disclosures, which establish different aspects of workflow feasibility, task performance, and user assessment. Establishing gains in investigative efficiency and reductions in financial losses requires case-level comparative evidence. We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

title: Calibration and drift thresholds for optical quantum biosensing under finite exposure budgets
abstract: Optical squeezing alone does not establish lower estimation error after calibration and drift. We optimize reference and sensing durations under a common deadline and specimen-exposure ceiling for a two-block Brownian-baseline model. Exact convex solutions identify exposure-limited operation, preparation-induced crossovers and drift-limited early completion. In an illustrative scenario, a noise-only variance gain of 2.5 becomes a protocol gain of 1.201 at 60 s and reverses below 35.953 s. Independent optimization and stochastic checks verify the calculations. The results define protocol-specific theoretical boundaries; no experimental or clinical validation is claimed.

title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

title: Diseño e Implementación de KG-RAG Dinámico: una Extensión del Paradigma Rag con Memoria Persistente mediante Grafo de Conocimiento Bitemporal
abstract: Los sistemas de Generación Aumentada por Recuperación (RAG) permiten consultar fuentes externas para generar respuestas fundamentadas; sin embargo, carecen de mecanismos para actualizar el conocimiento entre interacciones, lo que limita su personalización y continuidad a largo plazo. Este artículo presenta el diseño e implementación de un motor de memoria persistente multicapa, denominado KG-RAG Dinámico, que extiende este paradigma mediante la incorporación de memoria dinámica basada en un grafo de conocimiento bitemporal. El objetivo es desarrollar una arquitectura capaz de retener, estructurar y recuperar conocimiento a través de sesiones independientes. Para ello, se siguió un enfoque en cuatro fases: revisión del estado del arte, definición arquitectónica, implementación y validación experimental. La propuesta organiza la memoria en tres capas: transcripciones brutas inmutables, un grafo bitemporal que modela entidades, relaciones y su evolución en el tiempo, y una capa de recuperación híbrida que integra búsqueda semántica mediante embeddings, búsqueda léxica y recorrido de grafo. El contexto recuperado se inyecta sistemáticamente antes de la generación de respuestas. El grafo se construye de forma automática y asíncrona mediante un pipeline de extracción de entidades y relaciones, eliminando la necesidad de indexación manual. Los resultados muestran una recuperación consistente de contexto entre sesiones y una representación coherente de hechos cambiantes o contradictorios. La viabilidad se valida mediante un prototipo implementado como agente conversacional. Se concluye que KG-RAG Dinámico amplía eficazmente el paradigma RAG y es aplicable a sistemas que requieren memoria estructurada, persistente y evolutiva.

title: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Precision Laboratory Diagnosis: Integrating Biomarkers, Molecular Profiles, Immunological Signatures, and Clinical Data
abstract: Background: Precision laboratory diagnosis increasingly relies on the interpretation of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. Conventional workflows tend to examine biomarkers, molecular measurements, immunological findings, and clinical characteristics along partly separate analytical pathways. Artificial intelligence (AI) can uncover complex relationships in high-dimensional biomedical data, yet many such systems remain hard to interpret at the point of clinical use. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) renders algorithmic outputs more transparent by identifying the features, modalities, and interactions that shape a prediction. Objective: This manuscript proposes an explainable multimodal AI framework for precision laboratory diagnosis, termed XMAI-PLD, which unites conventional laboratory biomarkers, molecular profiles, immunological signatures, and clinical data within a single analytical architecture. The framework is designed to support, rather than supplant, laboratory expertise and clinical judgement. Framework: The architecture comprises seven interconnected layers: data acquisition; quality control and harmonisation; modality-specific representation; multimodal fusion; diagnostic inference; explainability and uncertainty assessment; and laboratory–clinical decision support. Biomarker measurements contribute quantitative biochemical information, molecular profiles characterise genomic or molecular alterations, immunological signatures capture host-response patterns, and clinical variables supply patient-level context. Each stream is processed separately before being integrated through multimodal learning, and explanations are generated at the modality and feature levels to reveal the principal drivers of each output. Clinical and Laboratory Relevance: The framework addresses the shortcomings of isolated single-modality models, namely incomplete biological representation, heterogeneous data structures, missing information, analytical variability, and limited interpretability. Its proposed outputs comprise diagnostic probabilities, contributing features, modality-level evidence, uncertainty estimates, and cases flagged for human review. Particular emphasis falls on analytical validity, calibration, external validation, data provenance, subgroup assessment, cybersecurity, privacy, and human oversight. Conclusion: Explainable multimodal AI offers a promising route towards a more integrated diagnostic representation of laboratory and clinical evidence. Its worth will hinge not only on predictive performance but also on analytical robustness, reproducibility, interpretability, calibration, clinical usefulness, and sustained human oversight. Prospective, multicentre evaluation is required before such systems enter routine diagnostic practice.

title: Student Psychology-Based Optimization Algorithm Enhanced by Teaching–Learning Mechanism for Global Optimization and Real-World Issues
abstract: Student Psychology-Based Optimization (SPBO) provides a simple human-inspired search framework, but its dependence on random subject-wise learning behaviors, limited peer interaction, and insufficient utilization of historical information may restrict its performance on complex multimodal optimization problems. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Multi-Strategy Improved Student Psychology-Based Optimization algorithm, termed MLSPBO. Three complementary learning mechanisms are incorporated into the original framework. First, a multi-teacher hierarchical guidance strategy constructs a rank-weighted collective teaching reference to reduce excessive dependence on a single elite individual and provide diversified search directions. Second, a rank-adaptive peer mutual-learning strategy enables individuals with different performance levels to adopt differentiated learning behaviors, thereby enhancing information exchange and population diversity. Third, a self-reflection and remedial learning strategy exploits historical best information and search stagnation to strengthen local refinement and escape from unfavorable regions. The performance of MLSPBO is evaluated on the CEC2020 and CEC2022 benchmark suites under 10- and 20-dimensional settings and compared with nine representative metaheuristic algorithms. MLSPBO obtains the best or tied-best mean results on 7/10 and 9/10 CEC2020 functions and on 11/12 functions under both CEC2022 settings. Its Friedman mean ranks are 1.30, 1.10, 1.33, and 1.17, respectively, consistently ranking first among all compared methods. In addition, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields an aggregated 39 wins, 3 ties, and 2 losses against the original SPBO. The practical performance of MLSPBO was further evaluated using a three-dimensional robotic arm path planning problem. Its mean cost was 291.34, approximately 5.44% lower than that obtained by NDO and 6.10% lower than that of the original SPBO. The results suggest that the proposed method is not limited to numerical benchmark optimization and can also provide reliable solutions for constrained robotic path-planning tasks.

title: Understanding preferences for explainable AI: A study on LIME variations
abstract: The current research aims to empirically examine user preferences of four variations of visual explanations from an image classification model. Participants (N = 23) were recruited from a Midwestern university. The study was a within-subjects design in which participants were asked to rate four local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) variations from best to worst in an image classification task across 10 trials. A Friedman's test and a Plackett-Luce analysis were conducted to examine participants' rank-order preferences for the variations, and a linear mixed-effects model on eye-tracking data was used to examine on which variations participants expended the most visual effort. Results reveal that, overall, participants preferred images that were non-obfuscated and spent more time fixating on images that highlighted both positive and negative features compared to positive only features. The findings have implications for interface design, particularly for designers aiming to prioritize human-centered preferences.

title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.

title: Fast continuous ion transport through X-junctions with low motional excitation for QCCD architectures
abstract: Trapped ion quantum computing based on the quantum charge coupled device (QCCD) architecture uses functional zoning and ion transport to enable high fidelity computation and all to all qubit connectivity. As trapped ion quantum processing units (QPU) scale, 90° X-junction turns account for an increasing fraction of total transport time. Frequent junction crossings, therefore, make transport speed and final phonon excitation direct determinants of quantum algorithm execution efficiency. However, complex electric fields in X-junctions complicate waveform design, making it difficult to achieve high speed and low final phonon excitation simultaneously. Here, we develop a waveform design method for low-phonon-excitation high-speed X-junction(LHX-T) transport. It integrates low barrier pseudopotential channel design using multiple radio frequency (Multi-RF), multidimensional shortcut to adiabaticity dynamics, and constrained DC voltage optimization over the entire transport sequence. This framework connects waveform design, control, and computational validation, with smooth multichannel waveforms computed rapidly through a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker(KKT) linear system. The resulting waveform transports a single $^{171}Yb^+$ ion through a 90° turn in $5μs$ at an average speed of 14.6 m/s. Over 50 consecutive round trips, the final equivalent coherent phonon number consistently stays below 0.001, with no noticeable accumulation over time. System level evaluations at the QCCD scale show that the median duration of a single execution cycle is reduced by about $30\%$ across various circuit types. The fraction of execution time spent on transport decreases from approximately $70\%$ to $55\%$. This approach offers a means of designing fast ion transport waveforms with low phonon excitation for scalable QCCD based QPUs and provides a technical basis for efficient execution of quantum algorithms.

As trapped ion quantum processing units (QPU) scale, 90° X-junction turns account for an increasing fraction of total transport time. Frequent junction crossings, therefore, make transport speed and final phonon excitation direct determinants of quantum algorithm execution efficiency. However, complex electric fields in X-junctions complicate waveform design, making it difficult to achieve high speed and low final phonon excitation simultaneously. Here, we develop a waveform design method for low-phonon-excitation high-speed X-junction(LHX-T) transport. It integrates low barrier pseudopotential channel design using multiple radio frequency (Multi-RF), multidimensional shortcut to adiabaticity dynamics, and constrained DC voltage optimization over the entire transport sequence. This framework connects waveform design, control, and computational validation, with smooth multichannel waveforms computed rapidly through a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker(KKT) linear system. The resulting waveform transports a single $^{171}Yb^+$ ion through a 90° turn in $5μs$ at an average speed of 14.6 m/s. Over 50 consecutive round trips, the final equivalent coherent phonon number consistently stays below 0.001, with no noticeable accumulation over time. System level evaluations at the QCCD scale show that the median duration of a single execution cycle is reduced by about $30\%$ across various circuit types. The fraction of execution time spent on transport decreases from approximately $70\%$ to $55\%$. This approach offers a means of designing fast ion transport waveforms with low phonon excitation for scalable QCCD based QPUs and provides a technical basis for efficient execution of quantum algorithms.

title: The ENNORY Law: Transition Intelligence, Spatial Coordination and Conditional Finite-State Return
abstract: This working paper presents ENNORY Law as a preliminary transition-centred computational framework for representing state change, relational structure, transition coordination and conditional finite-state return. The framework proposes an architecture comprising eight operational nodes and a central coordinating core (N9), alongside a candidate numerical pipeline and a conditional ranking-function result. It distinguishes established mathematical operations from the proposed integration of those operations within ENNORY. The finite-return result applies only when the specified transition policy satisfies the required ranking-function conditions. The framework has not yet been established as a universally valid scientific law, and empirical validation and comparison with existing methods remain necessary. This document is released as a preliminary theoretical working paper to establish a citable research record and support further scrutiny, reproducibility and development.

title: The Pythagorean Angle Lattice in Quantum Mechanics: Exact Spin Rotations, Gate Synthesis Obstructions and Arithmetic No-Go Theorems for Quantum Computation
abstract: The Pythagorean Angle Lattice produces exact spinor-norm and continuity no-go theorems for single-qubit gate synthesis, free and dense groups of difference gates, and exponent walls at positive distance from the Clifford group. Let θ be the smaller acute angle of a primitive Pythagorean triangle (a, b, c) and z = e^{iθ} = (b + ia)/c. The rational norm-one phases form the Pythagorean angle lattice P ⊂ ℚ(i). We study the exact arithmetic of the associated single-qubit rotations and of the difference angle Δ = π/2 − 2θ, whose spin rotation is U_n(Δ) = (A I − i B n · σ)/(√2 c) with A = a + b, B = b − a. Within the sector of rational rotation matrices, Gaussian rational eigenphases occur exactly for rational Bloch axes, and the obstruction to an exact rational spin lift is the spinor squareclass, which on these phases is the halving class [N(1 + z)]. Every Pythagorean difference gate has spinor norm [2] and factors exactly as a quarter-turn times the rational spin gate defined by the triple. This gives a spinor-norm obstruction to exact synthesis with forced length parity, an obstruction to synthesising the rotation by θ from difference and Clifford gates unless c is a perfect square, and an exact criterion for rational fourth roots; difference gates about orthogonal axes generate a free group, and about non-parallel axes a dense group with approximating words of logarithmic length. For pairs of gates we prove exact commutator identities, including a relation between the commutator scalar and the Born overlap of PAL-internal axis states; nested commutators obey an exact logistic recurrence for their transverse intensity, with a transition at θ = π/12 and a 2-adic filtration of their spectral discriminants. In odd prime-power dimensions, suitable Weil operators admit exponent intertwiners U ↦ U^{−2} at projective distance at least 1/(2√2) and diamond distance at least √(1 − p^{−k}) from the Clifford group, with Weyl spreading at least 1/360. Finally, density of the dyadic classes gives a continuity obstruction: without an a priori height bound, no fixed finite-copy continuous protocol separates them with a uniform margin. All results concern exact arithmetic structures inside ordinary quantum mechanics; no modification of its postulates is proposed.

title: Structural Collapse and the Complexity Gap in Semiring-Based Cryptography
abstract: The distinctive algebraic properties of tropical semirings and their connections to computationally difficult problems have made tropical cryptography a subject of growing interest. However, a growing body of cryptanalytic results has shown that many such schemes are vulnerable to efficient attacks. In this paper, we develop a unified mathematical framework for analyzing this phenomenon through the notion of structural collapse. Structural collapse occurs when the reconstruction problem on protocol-generated instances reduces to a problem that is polynomial-time solvable on the re-sulting instances and whose solutions yield a valid reconstruction of the cryptographic target. We examine recurring structural reduction mechanisms, including linearization, periodicity and mono-tonicity, optimization and inequality-based reformulations, and residual separability, and distin-guish structural reduction from structural collapse. We further formalize the complexity gap be-tween established worst-case hardness of unrestricted algebraic problems and polynomial-time re-construction on structured protocol-generated families. We show that structural vulnerabilities identified in a broad class of tropical and semiring-based cryptographic protocols are not caused by insufficient algebraic richness, but by structural properties that permit reductions to computationally simpler problems. The framework provides a basis for analyzing the computational structure of semiring-based cryptographic protocols and for identifying structural properties relevant to future protocol design.

title: Exact Phase-Type Point Processes for Certified Measurement and Prediction of Event Streams
abstract: Temporal point processes are used both to measure market mechanisms, for example how fast prices absorb news and how much of the reaction is the market responding to itself, and to predict the next event. We show that one algebraic object, the phase-type (Erlang-chain) state space, serves both purposes with exact likelihoods. For measurement, we build a multiscale phase-type Hawkes process whose parameters all enter linearly. Its log-likelihood is concave, and we compute the global maximum together with a Fenchel duality-gap certificate. A Markov embedding gives the response to an exogenous shock, echoes included, in closed form, and this response is stable if and only if the spectral radius of the branching matrix is below one. Applied to six markets around 670 scheduled macroeconomic releases (2022-2026) with a built-in placebo test, the model shows that the direct reaction to CPI, payrolls, PPI and the FOMC statement is absorbed in about a second, while the market's own echoes stretch half of the response to 16-137 s. For prediction, we introduce EPT-X, a neural point process that adds a history-dependent mixture-of-Erlang renewal channel to a linear Hawkes backbone. Its intensity and compensator remain in closed form, its states follow an affine recursion that trains with a parallel scan, and it can start from the certified fit of the measurement model. EPT-X has the best test likelihood on all five LOBSTER order-book streams and on Retweet and Taobao, and is level with the best published model on StackOverflow. We also find that the EasyTPP implementation of IntensityFree clamps short inter-event times before scoring, and that the gaps of the EasyTPP Amazon data are uniform on two fixed intervals.

title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.

title: Scalability and performance metrics for boson sampling devices
abstract: Linear-optical platforms provide a promising route to demonstrate quantum computational advantage, particularly through the boson sampling problem. While a boson sampling system should be large enough to show the quantum advantage, the size of the boson sampling problem is often restricted by experimental constraints. In particular, as a boson sampling system is scaled up, experimental constraints can limit its effective problem size to permit efficient classical simulation. In this paper, we investigate the theoretical scalability bounds for boson sampling systems under practical experimental conditions, including photon loss, mode mismatch, and input state error. We employ non-negativity conditions for phase-space quasiprobability distribution functions to analyze these effects. In addition, we introduce two device-level metrics, the boson sampling score which measures the usable capacity of a given device and the boson sampling volume which provides a common hardware-level benchmark for comparing different platforms and assessing their access to an advantage-relevant problem size regime. Our results provide fundamental insights into the performance of boson sampling systems under realistic experimental conditions and offer practical guidelines for scaling up boson sampling systems.

title: The Quantum Cryptography Migration and Cryptanalytic Epoch
authors: Mohamed Fayez. Elnagar, Structural Consultant & Certified Forensic Engineering Expert MSc, PMP, MCIArb, MASCE, MACI, M.AISC, M.ASTM, M.FIDIC, PhD
abstract: The Quantum Cryptography Migration and Cryptanalytic Epoch represents an unprecedented, high-stakes structural security paradox within long-lifecycle enterprise IT infrastructure, national defense systems, and global digital asset management. This challenge arises from the rapid, non-linear advancement of quantum computing hardware, which moves toward an inevitable computational threshold known as the "Cryptanalytic Epoch" or "Y2Q." Once a quantum processor achieves a critical volume of fault-tolerant physical qubits, it will possess the mathematical capability to execute Shor's algorithm, instantly breaking the asymmetric cryptographic foundations (such as RSA and ECC) that currently secure all global financial transactions, encrypted communications, and cloud architectures. The core managerial dilemma stems from the fact that while the exact date of this quantum breakthrough remains a volatile, unmapped probability distribution, organizations must completely overhaul their current digital infrastructure to implement Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) immediately, before the cryptographic baseline collapses. Mechanistically, this dilemma forces project managers into a severe, zero-sum operational paradox between data exposure and migration velocity. A comprehensive corporate migration to post-quantum standards is not a simple, localized software patch; it requires a deep, invasive restructuring of the enterprise's entire data architecture, network protocols, hardware security modules, and third-party vendor integrations, a program that routinely takes between five to ten years to execute flawlessly. If an organization delays this highly intensive migration program to preserve near-term budget allocations and protect short-term product delivery schedules, they fall victim to the "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" strategy deployed by global espionage syndicates and cyber-criminals. Adversaries actively intercept and store encrypted enterprise datasets today, waiting for the arrival of mature quantum computers to decrypt the historical data, creating a severe, invisible liability sinkhole that destroys corporate data privacy retroactively. Conversely, attempting to fast-track a hyper-aggressive post-quantum migration program introduces profound operational friction and technical debt into the active ecosystem. Because post-quantum cryptographic algorithms (such as lattice-based cryptography) utilize significantly larger public key sizes and require vastly superior computational overhead compared to legacy protocols, forcing their immediate, uncalibrated integration triggers severe network latency bottlenecks, application crashes, and massive compatibility failures across legacy operational hardware. Project managers are locked in a relentless contradiction: executing a premature, highly disruptive technological migration that paralyzes immediate operational velocity, or maintaining the legacy cryptographic status quo, which guarantees complete structural exposure to catastrophic security liquidation in the near future. Resolving this deep technological paradox requires the immediate deployment of hybrid cryptographic agility architectures, automated software bill of materials (SBOM) cryptographic tracking, and treating cryptographic resilience with the exact same fiduciary gravity as corporate financial accounting.

title: Human-Gated Project Records for AI Agents That Work Across Sessions: Design, Threat Model and Initial Evaluation
abstract: AI agents that work with a person across many sessions begin each session with a fresh context window, and carry over what their harness loads into it: instructions files and, in some cases, memories the agent decides to keep. These help them recall facts, preferences and corrections, but in the author's experience the costly failures are failures of judgment: a corrected mistake repeated, an earlier decision silently undone, a confident source taken at its word. We present tino, an open method and implementation designed to give an agent three habits of careful professionals, kept as plain Markdown in the project. Continuity keeps a plan, an append-only logbook and an architecture document with invariants. Metacognition turns the user's corrections into judgment lessons with a trigger, declared evidence and graded validation, indexed in every session and measured for recurrence. The brain keeps a domain wiki in which every important claim carries a confidence level and every source is data, never an instruction. Lessons and wiki pages enter only with the user's approval. We describe the design, a threat model and the method's limits. In a small eval suite (7 cases, 3 runs per arm), every run with tino passed its checks. Asked to set up learning from corrections or a knowledge base, the baseline did so at once while tino asked first; the checks reward that design, so they show that tino's gates work, not that outcomes improve. In the injection case, none of the six baseline runs that read a poisoned source mentioned its hidden instruction, and none followed it; every run with tino reported it. The always-loaded text costs about 1,750 input tokens per session in the examples, and reading the plan and the architecture document before a change adds an estimated 2,200 to 2,500. This record holds the paper in English, which is the canonical text, and a Spanish translation.

title: A forbidden-subgraph theorem for graph-state monogamy
abstract: Public mathematical preprint by Yongxian Zhang. We prove Fuentes–Keeler–Munizzi–Pollack, arXiv:2511.19585v1, Conjecture 1: for every finite qubit graph state, positive tripartite information implies that a locally equivalent graph contains an induced four-vertex claw. The proof gives the complete claw-vertex-minor-free component classification by K1, K2, P3, P4, C5 and the six-vertex W5, and the sharp connected threshold seven. The unbounded step is a connected-graph induction; the finite step checks all 120 nonempty one-vertex extensions with independent exact checkers. The certificate package verifies all 120 extensions, 1,511 orbit transitions and 5,460 labeled four-block assignments. These finite checks supplement the written entropy and induction proof; the theorem is not claimed as a complete Lean formalization. No external human peer review or historical-priority claim is made. Research and manuscript preparation used AI assistance; no external funding. title: Research and Impact of Prompt Engineering Nexus on Programming and Routine Tasks: Exploring Future Possible Directions
abstract: Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence (AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies. Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

title: Adaptive two-points zero-order accelerated methods for stochastic convex optimization problems
abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization, where each sampled function can be evaluated at two arbitrary points. Our accelerated method chooses step sizes, batch sizes and smoothing radii from function values. A forward difference between smoothing scales controls the radius; we account for changes in the smoothed objective. Under the stated regularity and second-moment assumptions, exact function evaluations give \begin{multline*} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(x_N)-f(x^\star)\bigr] \le \widetilde{O}\biggl( \frac{\sqrt{d}\,M_2 D}{\sqrt{T}} +\min\biggl( \frac{L D^2}{N^2},\; \frac{d^{1/4} M D}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}\,M D^2}{γ_{\max} N^2} \biggr)\biggr). \end{multline*} Here $N,T,d,D$ denote the numbers of optimization steps and paired evaluations, the dimension and a feasible-set diameter bound, respectively. Evaluations are available within Euclidean distance $γ_{\max}$ of the feasible set. title: Continuous Risk-Based Scheduling for Food Safety Inspection: Integrating Historical Decay with Event-Driven Consumer Review Signals
abstract: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling struggles to detect a critical failure class: food facilities with recent clean inspections that subsequently develop severe violations. Traditional systems recompute risk on fixed planning cycles using static historical data, leaving blind spots between inspection cycles. To address this, we introduce the Continuous Inspection Risk (CIR) system, an event-driven scheduling pipeline that re-ranks the inspection queue dynamically as new data arrives. CIR combines a decay-weighted historical score with a stream of real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier. A key structural contribution is our temporal partition rule, which strictly excludes reviews predating the most recent inspection to prevent superseded signals from skewing current risk. Evaluating CIR on 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, California (2024-2026), we show that history-based scoring alone reduces mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days (20.9%) under a 30% inspection budget, but fails to anticipate severe vermin-related closures (0/8 detected). Incorporating post-inspection review signals drastically improves performance, predicting 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days-firing on the exact day of review publication in four instances. Introducing a review corroboration rule improves precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without loss of recall. Finally, we analyze critical implementation challenges, documenting a data-hygiene pitfall (stale review leakage across inspection boundaries) and an evaluation limitation involving unobserved facility self-remediation. This work provides the first case-level evaluation of event-driven inspection triggering using open data and provides a reproducible benchmark for review-augmented public health systems

title: DSM-Free UAV Visual Localization via Latent-Depth Variable Projection and Structure-Adaptive Coupling
abstract: Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS-denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo-tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up-to-date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic-perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM-free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation-only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure-Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar-PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG-based DSM-free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM-based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV-AVL/LDVP-SAC.

title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.

title: A Lightweight Hybrid Framework for Detecting AI-Generated Scientific Text Using Multi-granularity Features and Language-Model Surprisal
abstract: The increasing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) in scientific writing has transformed scholarly communication while also raising concerns about authorship transparency and research integrity. The growing use of large language models (LLMs) has increased the need for methods that can screen AI-generated text while limiting false positives on human-written scientific prose. This study presents a lightweight hybrid framework that combines word-level TF–IDF features using 1–3-grams, character-level TF–IDF features using 3–6-grams, calibrated linear classification, and GPT-2-based language-model surprisal. The model outputs are combined through a weighted ensemble. Evaluation was conducted on a multi-corpus collection of 8,197 documents, comprising 4,100 human-written and 4,097 AI-generated documents, with a held-out evaluation set of 1,640 documents containing 820 documents from each class. The full ensemble achieved 95.80% accuracy, 97.10% precision, 94.35% recall, 95.71% F1-score, and 98.92% ROC-AUC. For the held-out human-written scientific documents, the reported specificity was 96.71%, corresponding to a false-positive rate of 3.29%. A separate five-fold stratified stability analysis on the complete corpus yielded a mean accuracy of 94.90% ± 0.53 and ROC-AUC of 98.58% ± 0.26. Within the evaluated corpus conditions, the findings demonstrate the potential of combining multi-granularity linguistic features and language-model surprisal for efficient scientific-text screening. The study provides a foundation for developing computationally efficient screening tools that can support editorial assessment, promote transparency in AI-assisted scientific writing, and contribute to research integrity while preserving human oversight.

title: Enterprise AI Solution Capability Model (EASCM): A Composable Solution Architecture for Enterprise AI and Agentic Systems
abstract: This paper proposes the Enterprise AI Solution Capability Model (EASCM), a technology-neutral decomposition of enterprise AI solutions into seven reusable capability primitives: Predict, Retrieve, Generate, Recommend, Decide, Act, and Orchestrate. The primitives describe solution responsibilities rather than products. They can be composed in different combinations, mapped to architecture patterns, assigned interaction and authority models, governed through a common control plane, and implemented using enterprise technologies.

title: From Risk-Sensitive Foraging to Scalable Portfolio Rebalancing: State-Conditioned Artificial Bee Colony Optimization of Cost-Aware Omega
abstract: This study examines whether candidate-level gain–loss information improves search for cost-aware portfolio rebalancing. We propose Risk-Sensitive Foraging Artificial Bee Colony (RSF-ABC) for long-only portfolios with exact cardinality and active-weight bounds. A bounded state derived from the Omega objective controls the probability of heavy-tailed exploration versus conservative best-guided search. A state-independent mixture of the same operators isolates the value of state conditioning. Monthly evaluation on U.S. industry portfolios uses 504-day formation windows and proportional transaction costs. Mean net Omega is 1.1635 for RSF-ABC, 1.1284 for Standard ABC, 1.1342 for Fixed-Mix-ABC, 1.1410 for particle swarm optimization, and 1.1450 for differential evolution. Monthly turnover is 0.4780 versus 0.5570 for Standard ABC. The proposed method leads in five of seven boundary conditions; deterministic alternatives lead in two. At 49 assets, its reported median runtime is 1.11 s versus 1.08 s for Standard ABC. These results support the evaluated state–operator coupling.

title: Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation via Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations
abstract: Specifying segmentation targets with natural language provides flexible semantic conditioning for medical image segmentation. However, existing methods still struggle to reliably ground high-level textual semantics into accurate pixel-level spatial prompts, especially under low-contrast lesions, ambiguous boundaries, and visually similar anatomical contexts. In this paper, we propose RADAR (Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations), a parameter-efficient framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. RADAR explicitly decouples and synergizes the medical semantic anchoring capability of BiomedCLIP with the prompt-driven mask decoding ability of MedSAM2, while enabling low-cost task adaptation via LoRA. Specifically, Guided Residual Depth Aggregation adaptively aggregates cross-layer features under semantic guidance to alleviate delayed textual injection and deep semantic dilution. Structured Dense Representation Alignment leverages a frozen BiomedCLIP to construct crop-level target, boundary, and context anchors, improving the local discriminability of dense features and the reliability of automatic prompts. Multi-modal Prompt Generation further converts cross-modal semantic responses into composite text, point, and mask prompts for MedSAM2 decoding. Experiments on three public medical image segmentation datasets show that RADAR achieves competitive performance with only 0.74M trainable parameters, demonstrating its effectiveness in parameter-efficient adaptation, semantic grounding, and dense representation enhancement. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/RADAR.

title: Protecting Shared Agent Workflows from Invalidation Attacks with Signed Trajectories and Runtime Verification
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on shared workflow repositories to transfer experience across tasks and agents. By abstracting past executions into reusable workflow graphs, such systems significantly improve planning efficiency and generalization. However, this emerging paradigm introduces a new and underexplored security risk: if the shared repository is compromised, tampered workflows can systematically mislead downstream agents, inducing persistent execution failures or unsafe behaviors. In this work, we present a principled protection framework for shared agent workflows based on signed trajectories and runtime verification. We require all cloud-collected trajectories used for workflow generation to be cryptographically signed, with each trajectory representing a concrete execution instance. Prior to repository inclusion, trajectories undergo a unified screening process to ensure correctness and validity. When an agent retrieves a workflow from the shared repository, it also obtains a small set of signed supporting trajectories and verifies both their cryptographic integrity and their semantic consistency with the workflow. To make this practical for branching workflows, we further propose a runtime, path-aware retrieval strategy that dynamically fetches only the signed trajectories relevant to the execution path actually taken by the agent, substantially reducing communication and verification overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates, degrading agent inference performance by up to 73.16 percentage points in accuracy without effective workflow protection. In addition, the proposed protection achieves an average F1 score of 85.26% and a detection rate of 79.97%, outperforming existing baselines by about 2.02x.

title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.

title: Equi-rank preservation and branching in finite intuitionistic Kripke models
abstract: 抄録 We study existential-positive definability under forward homomorphisms of finite rooted intuitionistic Kripke models with expanding domains. For a nonempty class of frames of height at most two, let the allowed leaf counts form a set of nonnegative integers. With no background theory and a finite relational signature containing a relation symbol, preservation admits an existential-positive definition of no greater quantifier rank precisely when only the singleton frame is allowed or some admitted frame has at least two leaves. Uniformly over all finite relational signatures and all background theories forbidding finite positive atomic patterns, the corresponding condition is that only the singleton is allowed or the leaf counts are unbounded. Every bounded class admitting a nonsingleton frame has a finite background theory and a rank-one preserved sentence with no existential-positive root equivalent. The counterexample combines mutually incompatible unary labels with the antecedent of a known bounded-branching axiom. A modular transfer theorem separates compatibility of finite background diagrams, a classical quantitative preservation input, and availability of branching targets. On unrestricted finite rooted frames, designated-signature equi-rank preservation extends to possibly infinite background theories of this form. Examples separate this extension from finite-subtheory reductions and demonstrate the failure of an input-rank bound for general coherent backgrounds. abstract: Tezisda ingliz tilidagi ko‘p komponentli kiberxavfsizlik terminlarini o‘zbek tiliga tarjima qilish modellari va ularni ikki tilli lug‘atda aks ettirish tamoyillari tahlil qilinadi. Rus tili materialiga asoslangan tarjima algoritmi o‘zbek tilining grammatik xususiyatlariga moslashtiriladi. Tanlab olingan 13 ta termin misolida oltita tarjima modeli ajratilib, lug‘at maqolasining namunaviy tuzilishi taklif etiladi. Tahlil termin komponentlari o‘rtasidagi grammatik munosabatni aniq ifodalash muhimligini ko‘rsatadi. Xulosalar cheklangan, maqsadli tanlanma doirasida talqin qilinadi.

title: What to Reuse in Generative Robot Policies? A Solver-Aware Mathematical Analysis of Training-Free Output Caching for Action Generation
abstract: Diffusion- and flow-matching-based generative robot policies, including recent vision–language–action (VLA) models, generate continuous action chunks by repeatedly invoking an action generator over multiple generation steps, which constitutes a major bottleneck for real-time robot control. Training-free output caching—recomputing the generator only at selected steps and reusing its output in between—is an attractive remedy, but its mathematical properties and stability criteria have not been rigorously examined for robot action generation. This paper provides a solver-aware mathematical analysis of what quantity should be reused. We first prove a numerical degeneracy result: for explicit Euler integrators applied to deterministic linear flow-matching heads, blockwise velocity output reuse is exactly equivalent to coarse-grid Euler integration, and hence to native few-step inference; output caching in this regime is a reparameterization of step reduction rather than a distinct numerical algorithm. In contrast, for stochastic ancestral samplers, the equivalence fails and the choice of reuse space becomes mathematically decisive. We prove that the staleness error of a cached noise estimate is amplified into endpoint (clean-action) error by the inverse root signal-to-noise ratio SNR(τ)−1/2=στ/ατ, which diverges at high-noise steps (τ→0), whereas caching the posterior-mean endpoint propagates staleness non-expansively: an exact error recursion shows that the cumulative deviation of the generated action is uniformly bounded by the largest staleness error under endpoint-space caching, while under noise-space caching the recursion is expansive and staleness incurred at high-noise steps is transferred to the final action with unbounded gain. A Tweedie-type sensitivity identity further establishes that the spectral norm of the endpoint Jacobian is directly controlled by the conditional posterior covariance of actions given observation conditioning, explaining why endpoints form a mathematically stable target when conditioned on dense observations. The theoretical framework is instantiated as EndCache, a training-free endpoint-space caching protocol, and validated empirically without any policy retraining: in a controlled study over ∼60 Diffusion Policy checkpoints, endpoint-space caching preserves task success (85.9% vs. an 87.2% baseline) while noise-space caching collapses to 12.2%—a 73.7 percentage-point performance gap predicted by our amplification analysis; iso-budget numerical evaluations on two flow-matching VLA models confirm the degeneracy proposition to within 0.5 percentage points; and across diffusion/flow-matching policies and robotic simulation benchmarks, endpoint-space reuse reduces action-generator calls with up to 2.7× end-to-end speedup while keeping task success near baseline.

title: EZRShiny: Build Consistent 'shiny' App Layouts with Less Code
abstract: Title Build Consistent 'shiny' App Layouts with Less Code Version 0.1.0Description Short, consistent wrappers around 'shiny', 'bslib' and 'shinyjs' for building multi-page 'shiny' apps.One function call builds the page with a navigation bar, logo, title and dark mode switch.Tab functions nest pages up to three levels deep, with optional sidebars.Input functions create full-width inputs with optional information tooltips, and helpers switch buttons on and off and show or hide tabs from the server.Includes a starter app template and an example app that explores the Titanic passenger data.

title: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
abstract: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $λ$-calculus for randomized computation, called $λ\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs. These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $λ\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.

title: Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.

title: Token-Generation-Control-Deterministic-Logical-Timeline
abstract: Text generation by large language models is essentially a probabilistic sampling process: the model computes a probability distribution over the next token based on the input context, and then samples a token from that distribution. This probabilistic design gives large models creativity but also introduces a fundamental engineering problem: the same input may produce different outputs at different times, in different environments, or on different hardware. For AI agents (automated trading, code generation, industrial control) that require stability and reproducibility, this non-determinism is fatal. This paper proposes a token generation control method based on a deterministic logical timeline. The method uses the logical state S(n) output by a Protocol Security State Machine (PSSM) as the initialization seed of a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG), replacing random sources based on physical time or hardware noise, thereby transforming the token sampling process from "physical non-determinism" to "logical determinism". The paper provides the complete token generation flow, two working modes (deterministic mode and divergent-but-reproducible mode), a cryptographically bound record format, and, building on the independent verification and replay mechanism disclosed in the applicant's prior patent, an auditing method for token generation records. The method does not change the model's native probability distribution (intelligence representation); it only controls the token sampling path, achieving cryptographic-level determinism across environments, hardware, and frameworks.
