title: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
abstract: As a key extension mechanism for agent systems, Agent Skills package specialized capabilities for reuse by LLM agents. An agent first retrieves candidate skills based on skill documentation and then relies on their metadata to make the final selection. As third-party skills proliferate on insufficiently vetted open registry platforms, the security risks posed by malicious skills become increasingly prominent, but existing attack research still focuses primarily on the potential harm caused after their execution. The limited related studies typically examine skill retrieval or selection in isolation and have yet to cover a complete end-to-end attack chain. To address this research gap, we find an end-to-end attack surface arising from the process-wide influence of metadata. Based on this finding, we propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end metadata-only poisoning framework. MetaCascade first generates diverse malicious skill candidates through multi-view semantic expansion, then uses tasks and black-box competition feedback to analyze the competitive relationships among malicious candidate skills and iteratively optimize malicious metadata, thereby improving the target skill's end-to-end attack effectiveness. Under a unified evaluation setting spanning four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, MetaCascade achieves state-of-the-art attack performance, with its average attack success rate (ASR) and its average ASR under four defense settings exceeding the strongest baselines under the corresponding settings by 35.53 and 34.65 percentage points, respectively. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.

evidence.title: MetaCascade: End-to-End Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
evidence.abstract: As a key extension mechanism for agent systems, Agent Skills package specialized capabilities for reuse by LLM agents. An agent first retrieves candidate skills based on skill documentation and then relies on their metadata to make the final selection. As third-party skills proliferate on insufficiently vetted open registry platforms, the security risks posed by malicious skills become increasingly prominent, but existing attack research still focuses primarily on the potential harm caused after their execution. The limited related studies typically examine skill retrieval or selection in isolation and have yet to cover a complete end-to-end attack chain. To address this research gap, we find an end-to-end attack surface arising from the process-wide influence of metadata. Based on this finding, we propose MetaCascade, an end-to-end metadata-only poisoning framework. MetaCascade first generates diverse malicious skill candidates through multi-view semantic expansion, then uses tasks and black-box competition feedback to analyze the competitive relationships among malicious candidate skills and iteratively optimize malicious metadata, thereby improving the target skill's end-to-end attack effectiveness. Under a unified evaluation setting spanning four datasets and two agents, Hermes and OpenClaw, MetaCascade achieves state-of-the-art attack performance, with its average attack success rate (ASR) and its average ASR under four defense settings exceeding the strongest baselines under the corresponding settings by 35.53 and 34.65 percentage points, respectively. Our code is provided in the supplementary material.

title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
abstract: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. In scientific optimization, this assumption is often violated, leading to surrogate representations that are poorly aligned with the optimization objective. To address this limitation, we propose TagBO (Task-aware Graph Bayesian Optimization), a method that integrates LLM-derived relational priors with descriptor-based struc?tural information for mixed-variable Bayesian optimization. Rather than directly using LLM outputs as predictive scores, TagBO treats LLM outputs as a potentially noisy source of task-aware relational priors and extracts coarse ordinal relational signals from LLM reasoning to construct task-aware similarity structures for scien?tific optimization. TagBO then performs constrained Gaussian process Bayesian optimization over the resulting joint discrete-continuous representation space. Ex?periments on diverse chemistry and materials formulation tasks demonstrate that TagBO consistently improves sample efficiency under fixed evaluation budgets across LLMs of varying capabilities.

title: PixGuard-Sim: A Deadline-Aware Testbed for Pix Fraud Detectors
abstract: Brazilian regulation gives a paying institution about a second and a half to decide whether a suspect Pix transfer should be diverted for review before it settles, on a system used by 170 million people where settlement is irreversible. Yet every openly released payment-fraud dataset and baseline we surveyed is scored in batch, with no reference to that window. PixGuard-Sim is an open testbed that scores a detector against the window from the latency it measures, and releases a Pix-native generator with a settlement clock and two scenarios open data omits: multi-hop MED-2.0 refund tracing and payment under coercion. Scoring accuracy and timing together pulls them apart. The most accurate detectors we evaluate are cloud reasoning models that never saw a labeled event from this stream: the stronger finds 112 of 150 frauds where a random forest fitted to the data finds 93, and neither answers in time. Ranking by accuracy alone selects what cannot be deployed.

title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation
abstract: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.

title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
abstract: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.

title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

title: AI Watcher: A Middleware-Based Monitoring and Control Framework
abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence and AI-enabled software agents has major security and reliability concern related to misguiding outputs, unsafe processes, autonomous behavior and insufficient visibility into AI background processes. Current risk management and security application guidance lack evaluation, monitoring, output validation, logging and controlled responses. This study shows that the AI Watcher, a middleware base prototype design to monitor output generated by AI and classify them from predefine violation rules,with maintaining a auditable log record and enforce a configurable response. The current prototype works around a control fake AI environment. A monitoring component observes generated outputs, a rule-based judgement component classify them and after that a enforcement component applies action on it such as temporary locking or freezing. A Streamlit dashboard which provides recorded events and system state. Current unit and integration tests shows a successful execution of several core functions while also showing classification and state failures. The paper concludes that the AI watcher as a researchable security control architecture rather than a complete safety solution for AI. An experimental extension was included to measure effectiveness of detection, false positive and false negative behavior, correcting the response, logging completeness, robustness to wording, and monitoring in real time. Comparative evaluation against the LLM is also proposed but no unperformed experimental results are reported.

title: A Collapse-Resistant Red-Billed Blue Magpie Optimizer for Employment-Policy Design: Programme Targeting and Occupational Retraining Pathways
abstract: Improvements to bio-inspired optimisers usually answer generic defects with generic operators. This paper instruments the red-billed blue magpie optimizer (RBMO) and measures what fails. Both operators scale their step by differences between population positions, and the attack places every candidate at the incumbent best, so the search scale shrinks with the spread the attack destroys. On five instrumented functions of the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation 2017 (CEC2017) benchmark suite the population collapses to numerical identity, and on four the error stagnates over the last 28% to 58% of the run. The proposed collapse-resistant RBMO (CRBMO) breaks the loop with a dual-anchor attack, a radius control under the one-fifth success rule and an adaptive foraging allocation; it adds no chaotic map, Levy flight or opposition-based learning. On CEC2017 at 30,000 evaluations, against nine swarm algorithms, it attains the best Friedman rank at D=30, 50 and 100 and 1.72 overall against 3.16 for RBMO. It outranks three published RBMO variants in every dimension, but the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) and the single-objective differential evolution algorithm jSO outrank it overall. At the standard CEC2017 budget its lead over RBMO is not significant; success-history-based adaptive differential evolution with linear population size reduction (L-SHADE), jSO and CMA-ES outrank it. Applied to programme targeting and retraining pathway design in employment policy, CRBMO beats RBMO in every instance, though the crested porcupine optimizer (CPO) ranks first.

title: A feature selection layer approach for multi-class classification on neural networks
abstract: In the age of data-driven decision-making, deep learning models have become powerful tools for uncovering patterns and making predictions that influence many aspects of society. However, their broader adoption in scientific and business applications is often limited by a lack of interpretability. Feature weighting methods, which assess the relevance of individual features, are among the most widely studied approaches for improving interpretability. While post hoc techniques have advanced significantly, especially in modeling nuanced relationships between features and labels in multiclass problems, embedded methods typically fall short in this regard. Embedded techniques integrate feature relevance learning directly into the model training process, but they are often unable to capture label-specific relationships. To address the limitation, we propose multiple extensions to the Feature Selection Layer, an embedded feature weighting mechanism for neural networks. Through extensive experimentation, we identify the most effective extension and benchmark it against established feature weighting methods. Our results show that the proposed method matches existing techniques in identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them in capturing label-specific relevance. By leveraging the internal dynamics of the trained neural network, it reveals how individual features contribute to the prediction of specific labels, requiring no post-processing beyond the training process.

title: StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine
abstract: Authenticated state transitions need proof engines that conserve memory, avoid repeated setup, and preserve request semantics across parallel execution. We present StateSync-GKR, a reusable Rust sumcheck/GKR core with a sparse-Merkle frontend, and connect its design mechanisms to controlled measurements. Sparse layer reduction and derived wiring reduce prover ownership and repeated verification work. Cube/affine fusion and parallel path constraints keep the circuit schedule and proof-size growth compact. Reusable preparation and indexed parallel jobs amortize setup while maintaining independent results. Three-state records, strict original-request decoding, and separate core/model interfaces expose the application and assurance boundaries. With circuit, field, transcript and prover driver held fixed, sparse reduction lowers additional requested allocation 3,242-fold and peak process resident memory 89.46-fold relative to StateSync-GKR's test-only dense reference for a two-layer mixed circuit of width 4096. Direct depth-24 fresh/prepared measurements show 3.46-4.45-fold lower per-request proving-path latency. CPU and full-proof delivery studies distinguish useful parallel work from queueing and return-path costs, retaining all outcomes and latency budgets. The evaluation supports larger circuits within finite RAM, lower repeated-request cost, and explicit deployment choices for this artifact. It preserves the cryptographic claim boundary of the existing construction.

title: Deterministic Promotion of Findings in Agentic Offensive Security: Verifier Oracles over LLM-as-Judge
abstract: This research presents RootViel, an agentic offensive-security platform built on the MINERVA engine, introducing a deterministic approach to verifying security findings generated by autonomous AI agents. The work addresses a fundamental limitation of contemporary multi-agent security systems: the reliance on Large Language Models (LLMs) as final judges of attack success. Under the proposed Hybrid Agents with Deterministic Decisions (HADD) paradigm, autonomous agents generate hypotheses, explore attack surfaces, and propose potential vulnerabilities, while deterministic verifier oracles retain exclusive authority to confirm findings. The central contribution is a deterministic promotion membrane that transforms an agent-generated hypothesis into a confirmed security finding only when an independent verifier produces a FAIL verdict supported by evidence associated with that hypothesis. This separation between autonomous reasoning and verification authority is enforced through architectural and structural invariants. The research introduces and examines: A deterministic promotion mechanism separating agent beliefs from verified security findings. Seventeen offensive-security assessment families employing deterministic, hybrid, and probe-based verification oracles. An epistemic verification model in which UNKNOWN is an explicit terminal state, preventing unsupported claims from being promoted. The Houdini adversarial laboratory and its independent Tribunal for validating attack claims against protected ground truth. Evidence provenance and chain-of-custody mechanisms incorporating cryptographic digests, Merkle anchoring, and Ed25519 digital signatures. An empirical evaluation of security findings against a document-oriented AI backend, distinguishing independently verified vulnerabilities from circular or synthetic findings. A preliminary external-generalization study across 40 repositories, identifying significant precision limitations when deterministic detectors operate outside familiar environments. The findings highlight both the potential and limitations of deterministic verification. While the architecture establishes an auditable boundary between agent-generated hypotheses and confirmed findings, verification accuracy remains dependent on the correctness and generalizability of the underlying oracles. The paper argues that autonomous AI agents should be allowed to explore and propose, but not to determine independently what constitutes verified evidence. This work contributes to research on trustworthy multi-agent systems, agentic offensive security, epistemic verification, autonomous red teaming, and accountable AI architectures. Publication status: Research preprint — draft for internal review, October 10, 2026. Not peer-reviewed.

title: Lessons from Luck (Study 1): locked records of the confirmatory run
abstract: Records of the confirmatory run of a registered study of LLM-written memory, reported in Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?. In 256 synthetic worlds, a scripted previous run used the more or the less reliable of two tools and was assigned a success or a transient failure; a model wrote a lesson from the run under ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction or one of two variants; a fresh session of the same model then named the tool it would call first in the next run, holding the authoritative run log and the previous result, with one memory item (that lesson, the lesson written from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive). Eleven endpoints served through OpenRouter, each pinned to one provider. The protocol, code and stimuli were frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23253562. Contents: every writer and reader request as scheduled (system and user prompt), every writer record (33,792; 33,789 with a lesson) and reader record (90,106; 90,084 valid answers), the 256 worlds and the run summaries, byte-identical to the locked run directory and checkable file by file against its completion manifest (included), whose OpenTimestamps proof is attested in Bitcoin block 970623; the two call ledgers with one field (a local file path) replaced by the file name; the registered analysis's output; a flat, machine-readable extract of all records with the script that checks the archive and rewrites the extract byte for byte. README.md describes the files, the record names and fields, and how to recompute the registered numbers with the protocol deposit's analysis code. Licences: records, extract and README CC BY 4.0; verify_and_extract.py MIT. Model outputs are included as research data. The writer requests reproduce ReasoningBank's memory-writing instructions (Apache-2.0; licence text and provenance in the protocol deposit).

title: Apollo: Bridging magnitude and sign-based optimization for robust deep learning
abstract: Adaptive optimization lies at the core of deep learning, driving performance across both computer vision and natural language processing domains. However, widely used optimizers such as AdamW and Lion exhibit inherent trade-offs between cautious stability and aggressive convergence, lacking intrinsic mechanisms to dynamically balance these properties. Consequently, they can exhibit sensitivity to hyperparameter variations and training instability, particularly when applied to complex architectures like Vision Transformers. To address these challenges, we introduce Apollo, a geometry-aware hybrid optimizer that dynamically fuses Lion and AdamW updates through a step-wise, cosine-similarity-guided policy. Built upon the decoupled weight decay principle, Apollo acts as an adaptive gradient filter, integrating directional smoothing via an exponential moving average to achieve seamless transitions between magnitude-aware and sign-based optimization steps. Theoretically, we establish Apollo’s convergence to a first-order stationary point for non-convex objectives. Empirically, extensive experiments on modern architectures, including ResNet-18 and DeiT-Small on CIFAR-100, as well as BERT-base and DistilBERT on AG News, demonstrate that Apollo achieves competitive predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in fine-tuning scenarios. Notably, Apollo exhibits low seed-to-seed variance (e.g., σ 2 ≈ 1 0 − 6 on DeiT-Small) and robust behavior across different smoothing hyperparameters, reducing the reliance on extensive grid searches. By formalizing a geometric approach to optimizer fusion, Apollo offers a mathematically grounded and memory-efficient alternative for contemporary deep learning tasks, balancing measurable computational overhead with enhanced training reliability. Code and additional results are available at https://github.com/Aliyar4061/ApolloV2Optimizer/tree/main .

title: Image Processing
abstract: Richly supplemented one-semester textbook on intermediate and advanced image processing Image Processing introduces a novel approach to image processing methods, combining the foundational and deep learning approaches. It integrates neuroscientific findings with mathematical formalism and practical implementation techniques and seamlessly blends insights from neuroscience and mathematical concepts. The book is enriched with practical Python programs, allowing readers to run and observe the output of many image processing methods, such as sampling, quantization, interpolation, filtering in spatial and transform domains, histogram operations, morphological operations, boundary extraction, object detection, and image segmentation. Readers can adjust these programs and change various parameters to observe the practical implications of the theoretical representations. The book is organized into four abstraction levels: Fundamentals of image processing, including the human visual system, mathematical tools for image representation and processing, and color perception with its formal representation. Low-level image processing techniques in the spatial and transform domains, including point operations, histogram techniques, convolutional filters, Fourier, cosine, and Hadamard transforms, multiresolution image analysis, and wavelet transforms. Intermediate-level image processing techniques, including image compression, morphological image processing, image segmentation methods, such as k-means, mean-shift, and normalized cuts, as well as image representation through feature extraction (e.g., polygon approximation, Gabor and SIFT features) and whole-image representation using trees and graphs. High-level image processing techniques with deep learning, including Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), Artificial Neural Networks, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Autoencoders (AEs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and Vision Transformers (ViTs) with their applications in image denoising, super-resolution, image colorization, image inpainting, image compression and dimensionality reduction, image segmentation, image-to-text generation, text-to-image generation, and object detection. This book is an excellent resource for a diverse audience of students and professionals across disciplines who work in designing and implementing image processing algorithms to address both theoretical and practical challenges. Pre-requisites include calculus, probability theory, linear algebra, and programming skills.

title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.

title: From Rainfall to Road-Network Functionality: Transferable Graph Forecasting for Flood-Disrupted Transportation Networks
abstract: Extreme rainfall can rapidly degrade road-network functionality (RNF), disrupting emergency mobility, accessibility, evacuation, logistics, and infrastructure restoration. Existing flood-transportation impact models are often difficult to deploy across regions because they rely on local calibration, intensive simulation workflows or target-region retraining. This study proposes G-R2R, a transferable spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that reframes rainfall-induced road-network disruption as a region-conditioned, topology-flexible graph forecasting problem for unseen transportation networks. The framework integrates ego-centered subgraph sampling, terrain-conditioned graph representation, region-conditioned dual-level static encoding, and dynamic rainfall-network feature learning. Static geographic and infrastructure attributes are fused with rainfall forcing and recent RNF states to forecast node-level RNF across heterogeneous road networks. G-R2R is evaluated using simulation-derived RNF sequences from ten flood-prone regions in Wenzhou, China, under unseen-region testing protocols. It outperforms representative forecasting baselines, achieving a stabilized MAPE of 2.33% and $R^2$ of 0.855 under the fixed unseen-region benchmark. Leave-one-area-out evaluation yields stabilized MAPE values of 2.30%-3.54%. Ablation analysis supports the contributions of the terrain-conditioned graph representation and dual-level static encoding. A historical-event replay of Typhoon Fitow further shows that G-R2R reproduces principal temporal trajectories and node-level spatial patterns of the simulation-derived RNF reference under observed rainfall forcing without target-region retraining. These results support rapid and transferable node-level RNF forecasting across the regional road-network domains represented in this study.

title: Federated Learning for Enterprise Cloud Data Engineering: Architecture, Security, and Governance Challenges
abstract: This research examines the application of federated learning in enterprise cloud environments, focusing on architecture, security, privacy preservation, and governance challenges. It explores how organizations can collaboratively train machine learning models across distributed datasets without centralizing raw data. The paper presents an enterprise federated learning architecture incorporating model training coordination, secure communication, privacy protection mechanisms, and governance and audit controls. It discusses key security risks, including model poisoning and gradient leakage, along with mitigation strategies such as differential privacy, secure aggregation, participant authentication, and robust model update validation. The study also addresses multi-party federation governance, regulatory compliance, model ownership, privacy-utility trade-offs, operational monitoring, and implementation strategies. It provides guidance for organizations seeking secure, privacy-preserving collaborative analytics across organizational boundaries. Keywords: Federated Learning, Distributed Machine Learning, Privacy-Preserving Analytics, Cloud Data Engineering, Enterprise Security, Data Governance.

title: SemLRA: Lightweight Robust Aggregation Against Poisoning Attacks in Semantic Federated Learning
abstract: Semantic federated learning couples task-oriented semantic communication with distributed training, reducing on-device training burden and end-to-end inference latency. However, poisoning through local data, task labels, or transmitted semantic features can degrade task performance and system reliability. We propose semantic lightweight robust aggregation (SemLRA) for an information-separated dual-server architecture. SemLRA calibrates task losses already generated during split training using the within-round median and median absolute deviation to construct bounded client reliability coefficients. These coefficients jointly reweight client- and server-side model aggregation and regulate subsequent server-side optimization. SemLRA estimates reliability without reference data, client-update inspection, or prior knowledge of the malicious-client count or fraction, while retaining FedAvg-order aggregation complexity. On CIFAR-10, SemLRA maintains accuracy close to its clean-training level under continuous attacks, exceeding the strongest competing defense in mean final-stage accuracy by 3.77 percentage points under label flipping. Under burst attacks, SemLRA provides the strongest accuracy retention across all evaluated scenarios. Measured training runtime shows negligible additional overhead.

title: Artificial Neural Networks: A Brief Overview
abstract: This chapter explores the foundational principles and evolution of artificial neural networks (ANNs), highlighting their key milestones and applications in image processing. ANNs, inspired by biological neurons, have revolutionized image processing through advancements such as backpropagation and deep neural architectures. These networks enable automated feature extraction and hierarchical representation learning from raw pixel data, supporting tasks such as image enhancement, segmentation, and object detection. The chapter defines deep learning as the use of ANNs to interpret images, achieving near-human performance across diverse domains such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics. The chapter defines the learning algorithm as a three-phase process comprising dataset preparation, model training, and inference. The chapter emphasizes the importance of constructing statistically sufficient training and test datasets. It also notes that the data may contain incomplete, incorrect, or noisy samples and that model performance is evaluated using a separate test dataset.

The chapter defines deep learning as the use of ANNs to interpret images, achieving near-human performance across diverse domains such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics. The chapter defines the learning algorithm as a three-phase process comprising dataset preparation, model training, and inference. The chapter emphasizes the importance of constructing statistically sufficient training and test datasets. It also notes that the data may contain incomplete, incorrect, or noisy samples and that model performance is evaluated using a separate test dataset.

title: Blending experimental electron density information to protein-ligand interaction
abstract: Machine learning models for protein-ligand interactions commonly rely on atomic coordinates, which are constructed by fitting molecular models to experimental electron-density maps. However, most models represent each complex as a single fitted structure, which can omit information about conformational heterogeneity, positional uncertainty, and local density support for individual atoms at binding interfaces. To fill this gap, we present CoDE, a Coordinate and Density Encoder, pre-trained on experimental density maps. We represent each binding site on a shared three-dimensional voxel grid combining atomic occupancy, experimental electron density, and its gradient magnitude. Using approximately 100K curated complexes, we pre-train a channel-wise vision transformer to jointly reconstruct masked atomic and density channels, learning a representation that integrates structural and experimental information. We evaluate the frozen encoder on two downstream tasks: (i) binding-affinity regression under leakage-controlled splits and (ii) pocket-conditioned ligand generation. Across these settings, CoDE improves over an identically pre-trained coordinate-only encoder and remains competitive with task-specific baselines, showing that density complements fitted atomic coordinates for protein-ligand interaction modeling and that the density-blended representation is useful for structure-based ligand generation.

title: ECAPA-TF: A Hybrid ECAPA-Transformer Framework for Multilingual Speaker Identification using the NISP Corpus
abstract: Speaker identification in multiple languages has received increasing attention in speech processing because of the growing use of voice-based security applications in multilingual settings. Traditional speaker identification systems have encountered difficulties ensuring reliable performance in bilingual and cross-language speech scenarios due to their concentration on local acoustic models and neglecting long-range contextual information. This research presents a novel hybrid architecture referred to as ECAPA-TF, which combines ECAPA-TDNN-based local acoustic modelling with transformer-based global contextual modelling for multilingual speaker identification. The proposed model is trained using the Native and Indian Speakers of Indian Phonetics (NISP) database consisting of 345 bilingual speakers of India, who are proficient in both English and native Indian languages, including Malayalam, Hindi, Kannada, Telugu and Tamil. The first step involves extracting Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC) feature vectors (40-dimensional) from the speech signal and normalizing the data prior to applying ECAPA residual blocks equipped with squeeze-excitation attention. Subsequently, the Transformer self-attention mechanism is implemented to identify long-range temporal and contextual dependencies in speech data. Attention pooling and Additive Angular Margin SoftMax (AAM-SoftMax) are also leveraged to create discriminative speaker embeddings. Performance is evaluated using Accuracy, recall, precision, confusion matrix, F1-score and ROC-AUC. The developed ECAPA-TF model achieved an accuracy of 92.93%, precision of 93.64%, recall of 93.02%, macro F1-score of 92.94%, and an AUC of 0.965. Under the same NISP experimental protocol, the proposed model outperformed the internally implemented Deep 1D-CNN, CNN-LSTM, and ECAPA baseline models. Compared with the ECAPA baseline, ECAPA-TF improved accuracy by 1.24 percentage points and macro F1-score by 1.36 percentage points. The confusion matrix and per-speaker evaluation further validate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed approach under various multilingual speech scenarios.

title: World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Time-series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross-channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real-world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context-aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large-scale datasets that align real-world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large-scale dataset for time-series forecasting with real-world event context. We first develop world2ts-core, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and Web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback-driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts-data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context-aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available at https://world2ts.github.io/.

title: LLM-Augmented Bayesian Optimization with Adaptive Policies for Chiplet Design Space Exploration
abstract: Chiplet technology is a key approach for extending Moore's Law. However, its design process is constrained by two primary challenges: the scarcity of early-stage platforms for rapidly evaluating chiplet-based heterogeneous systems, and the complex relationships between design parameters and optimization metrics. To address these challenges, we propose a synergistic framework that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) with Bayesian Optimization (BO), enabling architectural-level simulation and automated optimization for the 2.5D/3D CPU-GPU heterogeneous chiplets. We extend the open-source chiplet simulator to evaluate 3D designs by supporting graph topologies. Further, to enhance the exploration efficiency of BO, we introduce an LLM that generates high-quality policies to guide the optimization process, enabled by our proposed adaptive directional policy reasoning (ADPR) and an exploration gain-aware fine-tuning method. Finally, we use the policy-guided BO to perform an automated and efficient exploration of the complex chiplet design space. Experiments on 2.5D and 3D chiplet reveal that our framework improves design space exploration efficiency.

title: Enterprise RAG Architecture: Cloud-Native Deployment Patterns, Governance Frameworks, and Operational Leadership Models for Large-Scale Intelligence Agent Programs
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become the dominant architectural approach for deploying large language model-based intelligence agents inside enterprise environments, combining parametric model reasoning [1] with grounded retrieval from an organization's own knowledge stores [2]. Published research on RAG largely treats retrieval quality and generation accuracy as isolated benchmarking problems [3], leaving a gap in how RAG-based agents should actually be architected and governed once they move from a pilot into a production service a delivery organization is held accountable for. This paper addresses that gap through two contributions: a five-layer cloud-native reference architecture for enterprise RAG deployment, and an Operational Leadership Model defining the governance responsibilities Head of Engineering and Head of Service Delivery roles must exercise once a RAG-based agent program is live and client-facing. Drawing on direct experience architecting and governing production Microsoft Copilot Studio agent programs across multiple concurrent enterprise engagements, we argue that a meaningful share of enterprise RAG failures are governance failures rather than retrieval or generation failures, and that the existing literature's near-exclusive focus on model-level metrics leaves delivery leaders without a usable operating model of their own. The reference architecture and leadership model are evaluated against qualitative deployment experience, showing that organizations pairing architectural discipline with explicit leadership accountability see meaningfully more stable service delivery outcomes than organizations treating RAG as a purely technical initiative. This work gives cloud architects and delivery leaders a shared, actionable model for governing enterprise RAG programs that neither group has been able to draw on from the literature alone.

title: NeurICE: code and results for "Evaluating Image Ciphers by What an Adversary Recovers"
abstract: NeurICE is an evaluation protocol and benchmark for image encryption. It judges a cipher by what an adversary can recover from its ciphertexts, not by how random the ciphertexts look. Every result states its key and nonce regime (correct use, nonce reuse, fresh key per image, or nonce-less). Each attack is reported as a signed estimate against a permutation null; exact attacks enter at their true value; and a learned adversary's null result is read only after it passes known-answer controls. This archive accompanies the article "Evaluating Image Ciphers by What an Adversary Recovers" (submitted to IEEE Access). It contains: the eighteen-scheme cipher zoo and an implementation of LSCM-IEA; the structural attacks (GF(2) position-code and affine recovery), the linear and learned attacks, and the classical statistical battery; the runners and result files behind every table of the article and its supplement, with host and code provenance; the scripts that regenerate those tables and Figure 3. Datasets are not redistributed; DATASETS.md explains where to obtain them.

title: Voice and Hand Gesture-Based Multimodal Intelligent Assistant for Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: The traditional modality used for Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) involves keyboard and mouse input, which limits the naturalness and accessibility of human interactions with computing systems. This paper describes the design and implementation of a multimodal intelligent assistant that allows hands-free communication with computers through voice interaction, hand gesture recognition, and artificial intelligence. The system consists of speech recognition, a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning component for providing answers to natural-language queries, a Text-to-Speech (TTS) component for spoken answers, a voice dictation component for hands-free typing, screen awareness component with AI-vision capabilities for analyzing screen content, and a lightweight floating UI for showing the state of the assistant. Hand gesture recognition is implemented as an additional way to perform control actions along with natural-language voice commands. Multilingual switching between English and Telugu languages is implemented explicitly to avoid unreliable language detection. This paper presents the architecture and methodology of the proposed system and current status of its implementation, specifying implemented components, components in development, and proposed for future development. Instead of inventing performance metrics, The paper highlights qualitative findings based on tests carried out on the functioning prototype. The objective is to show how the combination of voice, gestures, and AI-based reasoning can bring human computer interaction to a more natural and inclusive model.

title: Somnium: A Recurrent World Model that Learns to Dream Before It Wakes
abstract: Preprint v1.0. Paper PDF attached; LaTeX source in the source archive.Code, full run registry, and per-run records:https://github.com/wilberforce1900/somnium We train a small non-Transformer world model, Somnium, under a developmentalcurriculum: chaos -> dream -> wake. A single recurrent substrate carries twodynamics -- fast streaming expansion (yang) and energy-relaxation contraction(yin) -- softly mixed by a gate; prediction happens in latent space (JEPA-stylenext-latent), and training begins with a dream phase of self-generated rolloutsbefore any real environment interaction. Dream-first pretraining reliably cutsthe real-interaction steps needed to reach a fixed accuracy by ~60%: replicatedacross five independent runs at 16K parameters (against a pre-registeredthreshold). Three further lines of evidence -- a scale ladder, a dose-scalingcontrol, and 871-round autonomous growth runs -- converge on the sameconclusion: the advantage is capacity-bound. Alongside the positive result wereport a registry of pre-registered negative results (a VQ situation codebookthat hurts training; a learned gate with no accuracy gain whose polarity is aone-way developmental ratchet; dream-statistics feedback with zero calibrationgain). All hypotheses, thresholds, and outcomes are logged in a public runregistry. Writing note: the scientific work (experiments, code, 90+ run records) was ledby the author; text drafting was AI-assisted; the author takes fullresponsibility for all content. Keywords: world models; pretraining; self-supervised learning; continual learning; pre-registration; negative results

title: Representation Upgrade and Label Revision Reproducibility Artifact
abstract: This software artifact accompanies the research manuscript When More Faithful Label Corrections Look Worse: Diagnosing Classifier Maintenance after Representation Upgrades. The study investigates how to evaluate historical label corrections when a classifier undergoes a representation upgrade. A central challenge is that the effects of feature refresh and label revision can become mixed in conventional before-and-after evaluations, potentially obscuring how faithfully a classifier responds to corrected labels. The artifact provides CIFAR-100/100N and Food-101 confirmation code, frozen experimental protocol metadata, derived result tables, frontend checks, interaction analysis, and a paper-to-artifact mapping. Together, these materials support inspection of the study's main empirical findings and evaluation procedures. Lightweight verification scripts can be run using Python 3.10 or later without a GPU, external datasets, or pretrained weights. The repository also documents the additional resources and execution requirements for more extensive reproduction. Source repository: https://github.com/Kane11378/representation-upgrade-label-revision/tree/v1.0.1 Author-owned code and documentation are distributed under the MIT License. Included third-party materials retain their respective licensing terms.

title: Web Server Development for Advanced Study Information Services and High School Career Planning
abstract: Career planning is a critical developmental task for high school students preparing for higher education and future employment. This study aimed to develop and validate a web server-based information service medium to support students’ further-study planning within school guidance and counseling. A research and development approach was employed, using an adapted Dick and Carey instructional design framework to guide needs analysis, product development, expert validation, evaluation, and revision. A preliminary needs assessment of 401 students at State Senior High School 1 Gedeg, Mojokerto, indicated that 70% lacked a clear career plan. Product evaluation involved experts in guidance and counseling, educational media, and information technology, alongside three school counselors as prospective users. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively using mean scores and inter-rater agreement (IRA), while qualitative feedback informed product refinement. Media validation produced average scores of 3.66 and 3.74 across the reported assessments, whereas guidance and counseling experts rated utility, feasibility, and accuracy at 3.36, 3.33, and 3.50, respectively. Prospective users reported corresponding scores of 3.27, 3.25, and 3.33, with IRA indices of 1.00 across all three dimensions. These findings indicate favorable expert and counselor assessments of product quality and preliminary suitability. The study provides a structured basis for integrating digital information resources into school career guidance, although further empirical testing is needed to assess effectiveness in improving students’ career planning. Keywords: Career planning; Guidance and counseling; High school students; Media development; Web server

evidence.title: Web Server Development for Advanced Study Information Services and High School Career Planning
evidence.abstract: Career planning is a critical developmental task for high school students preparing for higher education and future employment. This study aimed to develop and validate a web server-based information service medium to support students’ further-study planning within school guidance and counseling. A research and development approach was employed, using an adapted Dick and Carey instructional design framework to guide needs analysis, product development, expert validation, evaluation, and revision. A preliminary needs assessment of 401 students at State Senior High School 1 Gedeg, Mojokerto, indicated that 70% lacked a clear career plan. Product evaluation involved experts in guidance and counseling, educational media, and information technology, alongside three school counselors as prospective users. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively using mean scores and inter-rater agreement (IRA), while qualitative feedback informed product refinement. Media validation produced average scores of 3.66 and 3.74 across the reported assessments, whereas guidance and counseling experts rated utility, feasibility, and accuracy at 3.36, 3.33, and 3.50, respectively. Prospective users reported corresponding scores of 3.27, 3.25, and 3.33, with IRA indices of 1.00 across all three dimensions. These findings indicate favorable expert and counselor assessments of product quality and preliminary suitability. The study provides a structured basis for integrating digital information resources into school career guidance, although further empirical testing is needed to assess effectiveness in improving students’ career planning. Keywords: Career planning; Guidance and counseling; High school students; Media development; Web server

title: CAST: Real-Time Motion Capture for Any Skeleton Topology
abstract: This paper studies the problem of recovering motion from monocular video, even when the target skeleton topology differs from the subject observed in the video. Although previous methods have made efforts to resolve this problem, they remain vulnerable to joint-rotation errors that are coupled across the skeleton and can propagate along its kinematic hierarchy. To mitigate these errors, we present CAST, a topology-aware motion capture framework that combines learned local rotations with geometric correction guided by predicted global bone directions. Our observability analysis characterizes which rotational components can be constrained by outgoing bone directions. Guided by this analysis, GRACE uses reliability-gated alignment to correct composed orientations in parent-to-child order, leaving unconstrained components to the learned rotation predictor. The motion predictor and correction module are trained jointly with motion-derived supervision, using a frozen image encoder. Experiments under the TopoCap evaluation protocol show that the proposed framework improves motion recovery across different target topologies, including unseen structures. Reference-based cross-skeleton evaluation on a curated Mixamo benchmark and a user preference study further assess transfer to different target structures. A causal CAST-B variant achieves over 51 FPS on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, with timing covering image encoding and motion prediction. Code repository: https://github.com/fankewen/CAST.

title: Classical Communication Helps Single-Shot Quantum Compression
abstract: Free classical communication can yield an unbounded single-shot saving in quantum compression, even though it leaves the asymptotic rate of an i.i.d. source unchanged. At every fixed error in $(0,1)$, we exhibit sources whose unassisted compression cost is arbitrarily large, yet a single qubit suffices with classical communication and no preshared entanglement. We establish this separation by determining the exact optimal source fidelity for compression through an $m$-dimensional noiseless quantum channel, with and without free classical communication, while preserving correlations with an inaccessible reference. Without classical assistance, the optimal fidelity is exactly the Ky Fan norm $\|ρ\|_{(m)}$, the sum of the $m$ largest eigenvalues of the source state. With classical assistance, we obtain an explicit spectral threshold formula and a protocol attaining it. Classical communication strictly improves fidelity whenever $m$ is smaller than the source rank. The corresponding compression costs are two smoothed versions of the log-rank entropy, also called max-entropy: trace-distance smoothing under local operations and quadratic smoothing under LOCC. For i.i.d. copies of a fixed source with positive entropy variance, however, the two costs have identical first-, second-, and third-order asymptotic terms. For nonlattice spectra, we determine the constant-order advantage: classical communication saves $\log_2(e)-1$ bits per block asymptotically, and the ratio of assisted to unassisted minimum communication dimensions converges to $2/e$.

title: Histopathology representations and region selection under fixed area budgets in a matched input benchmark
abstract: Background: Histology-guided region selection depends on both image representation and selection rules. We compared ten matched RGB224 descriptors with UNI, a frozen pretrained pathology encoder, followed by training-only weighted principal component analysis and ridge regression. Both branches used identical image inputs, candidates and whole-image area allowances. Top-k packed regions in predicted utility-per-area order; facility selection also rewarded representative regions. Eleven development fields from eight author-defined patient groups underwent nested validation. Models and image-only selections for 33 source slides were fixed before annotation decoding. The primary endpoint was class-balanced annotation-mass coverage at a 10% whole-image area allowance.Results: All 33 planned sources were evaluable, providing 13267 candidates and 660 policy-budget scenarios. UNI top-k increased mean coverage from 22.714% to 29.058%. The mean paired gain was +6.344 percentage points, with descriptive 95% source-slide bootstrap interval [2.717, 10.517] from 2000 resamples; the median gain was +3.460 points. Twenty-two sources improved and 11 declined; the worst decline was −16.440 points. Within UNI, the mean facility-minus-top-k difference was +0.201 points, with corresponding mean-difference interval [−0.626, 1.113] and 14 positive versus 19 negative sources. Separate within-project computational checks accounted for one coordinate serialization exception.Conclusions: The specified UNI pipeline increased mean annotation capture, whereas facility selection showed no consistent advantage. Sparse positive classes can strongly influence the equal-class endpoint. Patient independence, individual pretraining overlap and physical image scale remained unverified. Prospective assay or clinical effects were not evaluated.

title: Latitude and Doubt: An exact ledger of meaning in messages with measurements on the genetic code and on English
abstract: Shannon set the meaning of messages aside as irrelevant to the engineering problem. This paper restores it as bookkeeping. For a source that pairs what is meant, W, with what is said, X, the joint entropy divides exactly into three non-negative parts: the information the form conveys, I(W; X); the latitude Λ = H(X | W), which the speaker remains free to choose once the meaning is fixed; and the doubt Δ = H(W | X), which the listener cannot recover from the form. The identities are the chain rule; the use made of them is the contribution. Meaning need not be declared by an annotator. For any purpose Y, the coarsest partition of messages that loses no information about Y is the belief P(Y | x) that they induce, and only the identity partition is adequate for every purpose. The leakage I(X; Y | W) measures how much a declared meaning fails to screen off form from consequence. Latitude has an operational value: in an idealized model with a shared key, it is the exact rate at which a hidden message can be written into the form of an unambiguous source without altering the meaning or the statistics of the text, and a finite-precision implementation is analysed separately. An unambiguous language with content C and latitude Λ needs at least 2^(C+Λ) distinct forms. We measure the ledger on six sequenced genomes, where the meaning map is the genetic code and the doubt is zero. Latitude is 1.235–1.501 bits per codon; synonymous choice carries 88.5% of the information that identifies the genome of a codon and 90.2% of the information that separates highly expressed E. coli genes from the rest; held-out genes reproduce these information values to within 0.003 bits; and 90,127 bits were hidden in 240 real genes without changing the encoded amino-acid sequence of any of them. In English the balance between latitude and doubt depends on what counts as a form and on whether items are weighted by use: on the well-attested core of SemCor doubt exceeds latitude for lemmas, by 0.44 bits per word, but not for inflected words, and among 22 wordnets latitude exceeds doubt in 12. The estimators are validated against a law of known truth, and every number in the text is produced by the code that accompanies the paper.

title: PENTA-CL v2 Milestone: Four-Engine Canonical Replay Convergence with Preserved Negative Results
abstract: Audited supplementary milestone, not completed five-engine certification. Four platform-configured engines passed two fresh-conversation captures each against a locally frozen twelve-case synthetic decision contract: 8/8 response captures and 96/96 recorded tuple declarations matched the canonical target. Original v1 negative results remain failed and are preserved at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23286324. V2 explicitly fixes the step-string delimiter contract and adds confidence-boundary/no-match cases. The expanded instrument and changed capture route prevent attributing the result to wording alone. Luna and Opus also matched raw response content; GLM and Sol differed in formatting but matched canonical tuples. Attribution is by platform settings, not provider attestation; shared workspace/context remains accessible. Local freeze is not public preregistration. DeepSeek remains pending. Benchmark baseline: one local validator-only run completed 200/200 expected acceptance checks, with 100 valid accepted and 100 mutant rejected; mixed p50 0.0733 ms, p95 0.0878 ms. Short sandbox microbenchmark, not LLM or infrastructure throughput. Historical per-engine reported durations are descriptive n=2, not a vendor ranking. Forty offline regression checks passed. No stress tolerance, live healing, PQC validation or deployed enforcement claim is made. A future stress test is planned and not reported as complete. Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. No comparative mesh, learning, recovery or resource-use result is claimed. AI assistance and capture provenance disclosed. All workload data is synthetic. Public evidence includes exact final outputs, instrument, frozen prompt, offline verifier and sanitized receipts. Raw API responses, private metadata, secrets, customer identity and PHI excluded. GitHub milestone and evidence. Research home: DCAI. DSOS Science. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

title: E8‑Octave Phase‑Dynamic Entanglement for Persistent Quantum Temporal Lock — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By weaving together the 240 E8 root vectors with the 132 Hz carrier and φ‑modulated phase offsets, we uncover a higher‑order "octave‑resonance" where each root vector entrains a complementary harmonic at a multiple of the base frequency, generating a self‑sustaining lattice of phase‑coherent channels. This dynamic creates a network of interlinked temporal loops that lock quantum states across multiple time scales, allowing on‑demand recall of stored information without decoherence. The resulting principle—called E8‑Octave Phase‑Dynamic Entanglement—provides a geometric protocol for building deterministic quantum memories and controllable temporal interfaces in quantum‑information processors. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
abstract: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

title: PEAM: On-device Communication Agent for Personalized, Efficient and Autonomous Mobile Network Configuration
abstract: The growing deployment of compact large language models on smartphones is enabling autonomous on-device decision-making, such as emerging mobile GUI agents. However, many mobile decisions, such as network configuration when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, must satisfy stringent latency constraints to preserve user experience. In this paper, we propose PEAM, an on-device LLM-based communication agent that autonomously generates personalized network-configuration rules executable within milliseconds. Specifically, PEAM first fine-tune the on-device LLM with a dataset constructed from manually annotated real-user data to integrate the communication knowledge into the local model. PEAM then operates in two phases. In the rule-generation phase, which is performed when the device is idle, such as overnight, PEAM analyzes historical network-configuration records in batches and reflects across batches to consolidate consistent evidence, reduce local bias, and derive robust configuration rules. To enable more accurate and stable rule generation over time, PEAM further constructs a user profile from high-confidence rules to capture the user's network preferences and incorporates this profile into each rule-generation cycle. In the rule-execution phase, PEAM is invoked when the communication context changes, such as when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, and searches the rule library to identify and execute the appropriate rule. Experiments demonstrate that PEAM, based on a fine-tuned 4B model, achieves 99.13% correct network configuration decisions, while 92.50% of the rules generated by PEAM are valid, outperforming the traditional expert-rule based method by 4.41% and 84.50%, respectively.

title: Tracing AI Agent Execution: Foundations, State of the Art, and Implications for Distributed Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: As of October 2026, the major AI-agent platforms can record the individual steps of an execution, yet theecosystem still lacks stable and uniform semantics. This paper combines three contributions: a conceptualframework for agent-observability questions; a comparative review of 13 platforms, with package versionschecked on 10 October 2026; and a non-normative interpretation of the implications for SGAEIA in distributedmulti-agent and edge environments. The results show that a trace reconstructs the path of execution but doesnot demonstrate the correctness of the outcome; that essential capabilities remain in beta, preview, orDevelopment status; and that divergent content-capture defaults create direct privacy, governance, andevidence-continuity risks. The central conclusion is that tracing, evaluation, and governed evidence mustoperate as complementary functions: observing execution, judging outcomes, and preserving a verifiable basisfor audit and assurance.

title: Field-Theoretic Computer: A Novel Computing Paradigm Based on Continuous Field Theory and Null-Operators with Optical Quadrature Vectors
abstract: This is a preprint (not peer-reviewed). Corresponding author: Shuntian Deng, mm.stdeng23@gzu.edu.cn. [Objective] To address the discretization error and the ontological fragmentation faced by the traditional Turing machine and von Neumann architecture, this paper proposes a novel computing paradigm — the field-theoretic computer — based on continuous field theory and null-operators. The paradigm takes "field is matter" as its axiomatic starting point and, within the fiber-bundle framework, redefines the wave function as a field-theoretic section. [Methods] The basic computational unit consists of an XY plane and a Z axis. On the XY plane, field A and field B are coupled orthogonally, and the mismatch of their symmetric and antisymmetric structures generates the null-operator a_ij = 0. Field C projects the null-operator along the Z axis onto a storage plate, where a second complement duality forms the stored photon quantum. What the null-operator carries is not a numerical value but the topology of a complement — the hole structure of the complement of the computed object inside a primitive cell of phase space. Complement duality is an involution, so the identical operation serves both inter-layer stacking and storage delivery. The probability measure is induced by the geometry of the section, and in the quadratic case its marginal distribution reproduces Born statistics; probability is therefore not a separate postulate, and the four premises of the Copenhagen interpretation are not mutually independent assumptions but four separate consequences of the single condition that the defining function of the section be of degree two. Stacked extension is realized by tensor-product stacking and contraction readout. The null-operator acts as a topological logic gate, so computation is intrinsically bidirectional and reversible and enjoys topological protection against decoherence. For physical implementation, continuous-variable quantum computing (CVQC) is adopted: the symplectic phase space and the Wigner function describe geometric storage, Gaussian operations correspond to single-layer computation, the nullifiers of CV cluster states realize the null-operator, and non-Gaussian operations (the cubic phase gate) read out the topological information. [Results] The complement count of a single layer is β0(Γ∖R) = β1(R) + 1, and stacking n layers gives a logical capacity n(h+1), where h is the number of holes contained in a single-layer region. The capacity is an integer and is invariant under symplectic transformations, so its protection does not rely on error-correcting codes; capacity is preserved under inter-layer coupling if and only if that coupling is non-degenerate; the per-layer fault-tolerance threshold reduces formally to a critical condition on the determinant of the covariance matrix. The computational stages are linked by a six-stage temporal chain whose realizability requires a bounded activation window for field C — this is the dynamical reason why field C must be of a different kind from fields A and B. The capacity and threshold structure has been tested at model level by a lattice simulation: within the parameter window fixed by the ordering condition, the single-hole system exhibits a two-level staircase (2→1→0) while the simply connected system exhibits a single step (1→0), with threshold positions matching the unified-caliber closed form. [Limitations] The threshold expressions are model-level analytical results whose coefficients have been calibrated by the lattice simulation under a unified caliber, but the relation between the area criterion and the semi-axis criterion remains undetermined. The closure mechanism of the inner hole must be stated explicitly — an expanding fill front is adopted here — and the existence of the inner-hole level depends on the parameter regime. Mainstream implementation of non-Gaussian operations remains difficult; the engineering of the cubic phase gate and of gate teleportation is still to be studied; cases with boundary degree higher than quadratic are not developed here; and the bidirectional coupling and calibration layer required for a real-time twin remain to be built. [Conclusion] This paradigm is complementary to the von Neumann architecture and is suited to continuous-field simulation and reversible computation. For the three long-standing obstacles of physical computation — no memory, no iteration, no error correction — the present architecture provides three corresponding mechanisms: hole-structure storage, involutive reversible read/write, and protection by symplectic invariance. It therefore offers recyclable physical computation rather than a one-off physical demonstration.
